newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-GrandMet/Guinness merger dash for growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-GrandMet/Guinness merger dash for growth.

text.p: British based food and drinks companies Grand Metropolitan Plc and Guinness will achieve much higher growth rates together than apart, joint chairmen Tony Greener and George Bull said on Monday in a conference call.
"It will create a combined spirits and wine company which will truly be a world leader so it will be able to grow faster at that stage than either would be able to do on its own," said Bull.
"If you put the whole lot together then you achieve a much faster growth rate together than either could achieve on their own," he said.

When asked about job losses, Greener said: "I really would make the point that the real reason for this merger is to raise the level of growth which will benefit shareholders and be exciting for all our employees."

Both chairmen said a hostile bid would have destroyed shareholder value. "We believe that both companies are property rated at this time, it's a no-premium merger so the benefit flows to both shareholders equally," said Greener.

Bull said he did not expect the merger to face any problems with the regulatory authorities, since the joint spirits business would give the group less than 10 percent of the world's accessible spirits market.
"The brands are also so complimentary, they fit like a hand in a glove, so there are very few areas of conflict," said Bull.

GrandMet's portfolio includes white spirits -- J&B, Smirnoff vodka, Bailey's, Malibu and Cinzano while Guinness is mainly in brown spirits like Johnnie Walker whisky and Bell's. GrandMet brands are dominant in Europe whereas Guinness is much stronger in the Far East.
GrandMet owns food business Pillsbury in North America and Burger King while Guinnness' other main business is brewing Guinness stout.
"We are entirely confident that will be able to obtain the agreement of regulatory authorities both here in Europe and also in the United States and elsewhere," said Bull.
"We have looked very carefully at the regulatory requirements and would not be here if we were not entirely confident we could satisfy those requirements," said Bull.
Greener declined to comment on the decision by Bernaud Arnault, chairman of French luxury goods conglomerate LVMH which owns a 14.2 percent stake in Guinness, to vote against the merger.
"The board of Guinness and GrandMet looked at all alternatives and we are absolutely convinced that the merger we are proposing is in the interests of all our shareholders," said Greener.
